name: Limbu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hildebrandt, Kristine A. 2007. Prosodic and grammatical domains in Limbu. Himalayan Linguistics 8: 1-34. DOI 10.5070/h98023041 (eScholarship open access). Corroborated by Michailovsky, Boyd. 2002. Introduction, Limbu-English Dictionary of the Mewa Khola Dialect, Kathmandu: Mandala Book Point, pp. ix-xi (HAL halshs-01883136); underlying primary van Driem, George. 1987. A Grammar of Limbu. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter, p. 15 (quoted by Hildebrandt, not reachable).
catalog_locator: Hildebrandt 2007: Sec. 3.2 p. 8 (feet/secondary stress), Sec. 3.3 p. 14 (examples 20-21, main stress on stem), Sec. 3.4 pp. 15-16 (example 22, prefix+stem exception). Michailovsky 2002: p. ix.
catalog_quote: Feet are bimoraic in Limbu, and a secondary stress is found on all non-initial feet. ... Van Driem notes that stress in Limbu is “not very pronounced and is non-distinctive,” but that verbal stems carry the (main) stress in stem-affix combinations (1987: 15). ... Note that in example (21) the stem still bears the single main stress, to the exclusion of the prefix. This non-initial main stress is different from (20), where the main stress does fall on the initial syllable of the word. This indicates that prefixes never bear main stress ... As described in section 3.3, in almost all cases, main stress falls on the stem, with optional secondary stress occurring on non-initial syllables, depending on foot structure and violations of Tautomorphemicity (cf. examples (10-11)). However, one case in which this does not happen is when the grammatical word consists of only a prefix + stem combination, as in (22): ... /ku-la:p/ ['kuˌla:p] 3POSS-wing ‘its wing’ ... In such cases where the word consists exclusively of a prefix and stem, the main stress will fall on the prefix, thus avoiding an iambic rhythm of weak-strong, which is unattested in Kiranti languages in general (Bickel 2003b).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Limbu is not in the catalog. Both title-hit items are Hildebrandt's Autotyp word-domains study: the 2007 Himalayan Linguistics paper (open access, already held by the project, read and verified) and its 2004 ICSTLL Lund talk (unpublished, no copy online, superseded by 2007). Hildebrandt 2007: 14-16 states, with van Driem 1987: 15 as primary source, that Limbu has a single weak, non-distinctive main stress on the verbal stem/root to the exclusion of prefixes and suffixes (e.g. ['tʰaŋˌŋaŋˌŋã:], [kɛ'siraˌdhaŋˌˌŋi:]), that a bare prefix+stem word stresses the prefix (['kuˌla:p]), and that secondary stress falls on non-initial bimoraic trochaic feet (p. 8). Michailovsky 2002: ix (Mewa Khola dialect) corroborates: roots accented, prefixes and suffixes unaccented. van Driem 1987 (DOI 10.1515/9783110846812, ISBN 9783110112825, phonology ch. pp. 1-19) remains paywalled; not in HathiTrust, Google Books and de Gruyter could not be reached by automated download; its p. 15 wording is known only via Hildebrandt. Weidert & Subba 1985 Rosetta excerpts (two newly saved), Tumbahang 2007 (Chhatthare) and LSI Sikkim 2009 are silent on stress placement. in updated with a dated search note. work relied on direct download/automated download and on-disk material.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Limbu has one weak, non-contrastive main stress per word, located on the (first syllable of the) stem/root; prefixes and suffixes are unstressed, so stress is word-initial in unprefixed words and non-initial after a prefix. Exception: in words consisting only of prefix + monosyllabic stem (e.g. ku-la:p 'its wing') main stress shifts to the prefix, giving a trochee. Independently corroborated first-hand by Michailovsky 2002: ix ('prefixes and suffixes are unaccented.. roots, which are accented').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Feet are bimoraic trochees; 'a secondary stress is found on all non-initial feet' (p. 8), surfacing only when a post-stem suffix/clitic is bimoraic and follows a consonant (with gemination, e.g. [a'njumˌme:]); light monomoraic suffix strings stay unfooted and unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefix + bare stem words take main stress on the prefix (['kuˌla:p]); van Driem (1987:15, as quoted) calls stress 'not very pronounced and non-distinctive'; Michailovsky 2002: xi notes some nouns syncopate their first syllable after a possessive prefix and others do not, 'possibly because of an accentual difference'.
new_statements.domain_note: Grammatical/phonological word (stem plus affixes and enclitics); Hildebrandt's transcriptions come from connected-speech LACITO recordings (Mewa Khola texts) plus van Driem's Phedappe citation forms; main-stress domain = prefix+stem, other P-word diagnostics = stem+suffixes.
new_statements.identity_note: Hildebrandt 2007 combines van Driem's Phedappe-dialect data (Tehrathum) with her own transcriptions of LACITO/Pangloss recordings of the Maiwa-Mewa Khola (Taplejung, 'Taplejunge/Tamarkhole') dialect; Michailovsky 2002 describes the Mewa Khola dialect. Tumbahang 2007 (silent on stress) describes Chhatthare Limbu, a divergent southern variety sometimes treated as a separate language but filed under limb1266 in Glottolog's bibliography. All fall under language-level limb1266.

sources.quote: In open (vowel-ending) syllables, length is generally determined by word accent and other factors: for example, prefixes and suffixes are unaccented and rather short compared to roots, which are accented. [p. ix] ... Other words, like nara 'face', do not undergo syncopation, possibly because of an accentual difference. [p. xi]
sources.locator: p. ix ('Vowels and vowel length'); p. xi ('Syncopation')
sources.note: Maiwa-Mewa dialect: roots are accented, prefixes and suffixes unaccented; accent conditions vowel length in open syllables and possibly syncopation. Agrees with Hildebrandt 2007 (stress on the root/stem).
